query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor interstitial carbon content into equiatomic NbMoTaW will activate additional deformation mechanisms—such as nano‐twinning and transformation‐induced plasticity (TRIP)—by leveraging the severe lattice distortion inherent to the multi-principal-element system, thereby improving room-temperature ductility without degrading high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW, a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy that exhibits excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor ductility at room temperature; its irradiation resistance has so far been supported mainly by first-principles calculations.
generation.intervention: Alloying the NbMoTaW system with a minor interstitial addition of carbon during processing to achieve a homogeneous, low-level carbon incorporation.
generation.conditions: Samples should be processed under controlled (e.g., vacuum or inert atmosphere) high-temperature melting and casting conditions to ensure homogeneous carbon distribution. Mechanical testing must be performed at room temperature (tensile or compressive tests), at 1600 °C for high-temperature mechanical performance, and via irradiation (ion irradiation to representative doses) to evaluate damage resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions induced by interstitial carbon that lower the barrier for activating nano-twinning and/or a limited strain-induced phase transformation (TRIP effect) within the BCC matrix, without forming extensive carbide precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The interstitial carbon atoms occupy small lattice sites and create local strain fields that promote the formation of nanoscale twins and possibly stimulate a minor deformation-induced phase change, while the inherent severe lattice distortion from the multi-principal-element mixing further supports these effects. This distributed activation of additional deformation modes leads to a more uniform plastic flow at room temperature; at high temperature, the overall BCC phase and solid-solution strengthening remain intact, and the defect recombination processes responsible for irradiation resistance are not compromised by the low carbon content.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated NbMoTaW, the carbon-modified alloy is expected to show a significant increase in room-temperature ductility (improved plastic strain and toughness), while maintaining comparable yield strength at 1600 °C and retaining similar irradiation damage behavior (i.e. no formation of deleterious irradiation-induced defects or carbides that might alter its resistance).
generation.baseline: Pristine equiatomic NbMoTaW RHEA without interstitial carbon.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only with very low carbon content (e.g., less than 1 at.%) to avoid precipitation of carbides that could compromise high-temperature stability or alter defect kinetics under irradiation; the processing route must ensure a uniform carbon distribution to preserve the overall BCC single-phase structure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in ductility and the long-term stability of the interstitial carbon at elevated temperatures remain to be experimentally verified. Furthermore, while literature on interstitial alloying in HEAs supports activation of TWIP/TRIP mechanisms, the exact impact on irradiation resistance in NbMoTaW needs dedicated study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW alloy samples: one set with a controlled interstitial carbon addition (e.g., ~0.5 at.% C) and a control set without carbon. Employ identical melting/casting and thermo-mechanical processing conditions to ensure homogeneity. Conduct room-temperature tensile (or compressive) tests to quantify ductility, perform high-temperature mechanical tests (at or near 1600 °C) to assess yield strength retention, and subject both sets to a controlled ion irradiation experiment (e.g., with Fe-ions up to a representative dose). Detailed microstructural analyses (TEM, APT) should be used to check for twin formation, phase stability, and defect evolution.
measurements: Room-temperature strain to failure and work-hardening behavior
High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance at 1600 °C
Irradiation-induced defect density and type via TEM or similar techniques
Microstructural confirmation of nano-twinning or TRIP features via high-resolution microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped NbMoTaW samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (i.e., increased plastic strain and enhanced deformation uniformity) compared to the baseline, or if there is any measurable degradation in high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation-induced defect structure compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

These improvements in mechanical properties of the iHEA compared to substitutional HEAs are due to the multiple strengthening mechanisms active in the new material. In the following we discuss these mechanisms for the case of the grain-refined iHEA in terms of EBSD (Fig. 4a), ECCI (Fig. 4b) and EDS (Fig. 4c) observations. The EBSD phase maps (Fig. 4a) show that the metastable f.c.c phase in the iHEA undergoes a strain-induced martensitic transformation from the f.c.c to the h.c.p phase as a primary deformation mechanism affecting the entire bulk matrix. The fraction of transformed h.c.p. phase at the necking stage (εloc = 90%) is 36.5% (in area%), which is much lower than that observed for the substitutional TRIP-DP-HEAs (area% >75%),. This observation shows that the f.c.c. phase in the iHEA has a higher stability than in the TRIP-DP-HEA. Already during early uniform deformation (εloc = 10%), nano-twinning is observed in the iHEA as an essential additive deformation mechanism (Fig. 4b).
